scenes.tts: Every sense ends in the same currency: spikes that look alike. So how does a spike say what touched you, where, and how hard?
scenes.visual: Title card: What a Spike Means. Four sense organs (fingertip, eye, tongue, nose) each send an identical train of spikes along a nerve toward a brain outline. Question on screen: what, where, how hard?
scenes.narration: Every sense ends in the same currency: spikes that look alike. So how does a spike say what touched you, where, and how hard?

scenes.tts: In nineteen twenty-six, Edgar Adrian and Ingveh Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor in a frog muscle. Then they hung weights on the muscle.
scenes.caption: In 1926, Edgar Adrian and Yngve Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor in a frog muscle. Then they hung weights on the muscle.
scenes.visual: A frog muscle strip with one stretch receptor and its single nerve fibre to an electrode. A weight hangs from the muscle. Label: reconstruction, Adrian and Zotterman, 1926.
scenes.narration: In 1926, Edgar Adrian and Yngve Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor in a frog muscle. Then they hung weights on the muscle.

scenes.tts: A heavier weight stretches the receptor more. Will its spikes get bigger, or will they come more often?
scenes.visual: On-screen question: Heavier weight: bigger spikes, or more spikes? Two candidate traces side by side, one with taller spikes, one with denser spikes, both greyed out.
scenes.narration: A heavier weight stretches the receptor more. Will its spikes get bigger, or will they come more often?

scenes.tts: They come more often. Every spike stays the same size. And while a weight is held, the firing slowly falls.
scenes.visual: Animated reconstruction labelled as such: three loads, three spike trains of identical height, spikes closer together under the heavier load. During a held load the spacing slowly widens. Labels: rate coding, adaptation.
scenes.narration: They come more often. Every spike stays the same size. And while a weight is held, the firing slowly falls.

scenes.tts: So the rate tells you how much.
scenes.visual: A rate meter rising with load. Beside it a bundle of fibres, with more fibres lighting up as the stimulus grows. Label: how much = rate, and number of active fibres.
scenes.narration: So the rate tells you how much.

scenes.tts: Now the what. Pressure on the closed eye is seen as light. Activity in the optic nerve means light, whatever started it. So the kind of sense comes from the line. Whether every quality works this way is still argued.
scenes.visual: Diagram of a closed eye with a fingertip pressing on the lid. The optic nerve lights up, and a light symbol arrives at the brain. Labels: labelled line; the classic example behind Müller's law of specific nerve energies.
scenes.narration: Now the what. Pressure on the closed eye is seen as light. Activity in the optic nerve means light, whatever started it. So the kind of sense comes from the line. Whether every quality works this way is still argued.

scenes.tts: A tuning curve plots a neuron's mean firing rate against one feature of the stimulus. The count varies from trial to trial. That spread is noise.
scenes.visual: A bell-shaped tuning curve of firing rate against bar orientation. Error bars of equal size appear on each point. Labels: tuning curve, noise (spread of the count from trial to trial).
scenes.narration: A tuning curve plots a neuron's mean firing rate against one feature of the stimulus. The count varies from trial to trial. That spread is noise.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea, for spikes counted over a fixed time. On each trial, a neuron's rate is its tuning curve, read at the stimulus, plus a fluctuation that averages to zero.
scenes.visual: Boxed text builds: rate = tuning curve(stimulus) + fluctuation. Beneath it: noise = the fluctuation's standard deviation. Small label on the box: rate code, spikes counted in a fixed window.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea, for spikes counted over a fixed time. On each trial, a neuron's rate is its tuning curve, read at the stimulus, plus a fluctuation that averages to zero.

scenes.tts: Which neurons respond, and their relative firing rates, together tell you what, where and how much.
scenes.visual: The box adds one line: neuron identities + relative rates: information about what, where and how much.
scenes.narration: Which neurons respond, and their relative firing rates, together tell you what, where and how much.

scenes.tts: A small change is easiest to see where the rate changes a lot, compared with the noise. Spike timing can carry information too.
scenes.visual: The box adds: small change: easiest to tell apart where the mean rate changes a lot compared with the noise. A footnote below: spike timing can carry information too.
scenes.narration: A small change is easiest to see where the rate changes a lot, compared with the noise. Spike timing can carry information too.

scenes.tts: How is the rate set? In touch, force opens channels, mostly in the nerve ending itself. In a simple model, each open channel pulls the balance point toward zero millivolts.
scenes.caption: How is the rate set? In touch, force opens channels, mostly in the nerve ending itself. In a simple model, each open channel pulls the balance point toward 0 mV.
scenes.visual: A touch ending with mechanically activated channels opening under force. A voltage scale with a balance-point marker, as in the action potential films, sliding from minus 65 toward 0 millivolts as channels open. Label: toy passive model; resting channels reverse at minus 65 mV; no injected current; settled voltages.
scenes.narration: How is the rate set? In touch, force opens channels, mostly in the nerve ending itself. In a simple model, each open channel pulls the balance point toward 0 mV.

scenes.tts: So the receptor potential is graded. Each extra channel moves it less, as the voltage nears zero.
scenes.caption: So the receptor potential is graded. Each extra channel moves it less, as the voltage nears 0 mV.
scenes.visual: The balance-point marker takes smaller and smaller steps as more channels open, approaching but never passing 0 millivolts. Label: graded, saturating (toy passive model).
scenes.narration: So the receptor potential is graded. Each extra channel moves it less, as the voltage nears 0 mV.

scenes.tts: But a graded potential fades as it spreads. To reach the spinal cord, it must become spikes, which regenerate.
scenes.visual: A graded potential shrinking as it spreads along an axon, label: about one length constant. Then a spike train that keeps its height all the way to the spinal cord.
scenes.narration: But a graded potential fades as it spreads. To reach the spinal cord, it must become spikes, which regenerate.

scenes.tts: Receptive fields help tell you where. Many afferents used for fine touch have small fields on a fingertip and larger ones elsewhere. Field size also depends on receptor type.
scenes.visual: A hand and a back side by side, each with outlined receptive fields: small ovals on the fingertip, large ones on the back. Label on the fingertip ovals: small-field touch afferents. A note: Pacinian afferents can have much broader fields.
scenes.narration: Receptive fields help tell you where. Many afferents used for fine touch have small fields on a fingertip and larger ones elsewhere. Field size also depends on receptor type.

scenes.tts: Endings are tuned in time, too. Rapidly adapting endings report change. Slowly adapting endings keep firing, and report the stimulus itself.
scenes.visual: A probe presses and holds the skin. Two spike rasters below: rapidly adapting, bursts at onset and offset only; slowly adapting, firing throughout the hold.
scenes.narration: Endings are tuned in time, too. Rapidly adapting endings report change. Slowly adapting endings keep firing, and report the stimulus itself.

scenes.tts: So a spike means what its neuron is tuned to. Next, neighbours compare.
scenes.visual: The guiding-idea box returns briefly, then a row of receptor units appears, teasing the next chapter. Text: a spike means what its neuron is tuned to.
scenes.narration: So a spike means what its neuron is tuned to. Next, neighbours compare.
